Its range is about four octaves, covering most of the vocal range, and the volume can be controlled in every register. Compared with the oboe, the clarinet handles wide melodic leaps more easily. Within the family the A clarinet is slightly warmer, the E♭ brighter, the bass clarinet deep and soft, and the alto clarinet close to the bass but less dark.

The clarinet is an aerophone woodwind, Hornbostel–Sachs number 422.211.2-71. Its body is nearly cylindrical, with a bell at the lower end and a single reed fixed at the mouthpiece; the player covers the mouthpiece with the lips and blows through the gap between reed and mouthpiece, which sets the reed vibrating and drives the air column inside the body. The clarinet family includes instruments of different sizes and pitches, commonly used in the orchestra, the wind band and the military band, and also found in classical, jazz, klezmer and other styles.

Modern playing usually has the reed facing down. The breath passes through the space between reed and mouthpiece, sets the reed vibrating and drives the air column in the tube. For a beginner the point is to keep the airstream steady and the lip pressure even, and to make sure no air leaks at the mouthpiece.
